albums.title: WHEELS UP
albums.description: Debut album. Eight tracks of pure 80s hip-hop built around one premise: movement is medicine, joy is a practice, and the roller rink is the most honest wellness facility ever built. 'Wheels Up' is a Saturday afternoon set — the kind that starts with the ritual of lacing your skates and ends with the glow of having given your body exactly what it needed. DJ Z does not theorize about wellness. He drops the needle and demonstrates. The 808 carries the argument. The Moog bass makes the case. The ARP synth stab signs the paperwork. This is 1983-1987 sonic territory — not nostalgia as costume, but as architectural vocabulary. The hip-hop of this period was built from the same conviction that powers this album: the body can be celebrated, community is built on a shared beat, and joy is not frivolous — it is foundational. Eight tracks. No filler. One continuous Saturday. And then — because DJ Z always has one more thing — a ninth track that should not work and works completely: the Oberheim power chord couples' skate ballad that the session earned.

albums.title: GLASS AND ASH
albums.description: Debut album. Ten tracks of Industrial-Hip-Hop, Jazz-Noir, and Dubstep built around one principle: pain released through craft, not volume. Named for the metallurgical byproduct — the impurities expelled from metal under heat before the metal can be true. Not darkness for shock. Not suffering as spectacle. The forging process itself: slow, pressurized, precise. This album does not proclaim hope or announce recovery. It stands at the threshold between the wound and the after and accurately describes the view from that specific position — because that accuracy is what the listener who has been carrying something for a long time finally needs. Industrial-Hip-Hop holds the rhythm of endurance. Jazz-Noir holds the harmony of loss. Dubstep holds the physics of what is embedded migrating toward the surface. These are not three genres spliced together — they are three languages for the same sustained experience. Ten tracks. No catharsis through noise. One arc that faces forward.

albums.title: YIELD
albums.description: Second album. Twelve tracks. The sequel to GLASS AND ASH begins where that record ended: at the threshold. Album 1 stood at the door and described the view. Album 2 walks through it — and discovers that the other side is not recovery. It is the beginning of something harder and more important: the choice to build. Surviving was instinct. Building is choice. The sound goes HEAVIER than anything in the catalog — the lowest tempos, the most crushing sub-bass, the densest industrial pressure. But the language goes SIMPLER — every hook is a phrase you could say to someone at 3AM when they need to hear one true thing. No hemoglobin. No biology lectures. 'Still here.' 'Hands.' 'We.' Words that anyone, anywhere, in any condition understands. The innovation: when sonics carry 50 tons, two syllables hit harder than twenty. The palette EXPANDS: industrial-hip-hop, jazz-noir, and dubstep remain the structural pillars, but reggae/dub enters for the first time — roots, patience, the rhythm of things that grow from below. The emotional arc evolves from 'I' (the solitary witness of Album 1) through 'you' (addressing someone for the first time) to 'we' (the discovery that the weight is shared). That pronoun journey is the album's backbone. Named for the metallurgical yield point — the stress beyond which metal permanently deforms — and for what a field produces, and for the act of surrendering what no longer serves. One word. Four meanings. Twelve tracks of the hardest, simplest, most globally relatable music the forge has ever produced.

albums.title: WICKED CLEAN
albums.description: Debut album. Twelve tracks built on one impossible premise: deliver the hardest, fastest, most intensely-cadenced rap album of 2026, and make every single syllable technically PG. Not 'clean version' — the ONLY version. There was never an explicit cut. The tension between delivery intensity and lyrical innocence is the entire art form. Aardvarco raps like he's getting away with something because the Boston accent eats consonants, the Twista-speed blurs syllables, and the Busta energy makes everything sound dangerous — but freeze any bar and it's about duck-duck-goose, clam chowder, parallel parking, or the specific joy of a potluck where everybody brought something real. 'WICKED CLEAN' is marketed with a Parental Advisory sticker that says 'PARENTAL ADVISORY: ACTUALLY CLEAN — we checked.' The philosophical core: each day is new, love is a choice you make every moment, unity is not a slogan but a practice, and the toughest thing a person can do in 2026 is choose joy without flinching. Beastie Boys party architecture. Mos Def lyrical consciousness. Twista velocity. Busta Rhymes theatricality. Atmosphere storytelling. Jurassic 5 underground craft. Eminem technical precision. 50 Cent hook magnetism. All of it filtered through a non-rhotic Boston accent so thick it should be classified as its own dialect. Downtown St. Paul spirit. Cambridge vocabulary. Dorchester heart. Twelve tracks. Zero profanity. One hundred percent that energy.

albums.title: NINE LIVES ON THE STRIP
albums.description: Debut album. Twelve tracks that answer a question nobody asked but everybody needed: what if the greatest hair-metal band of 1987 formed in St. Paul's Lowertown artist district in 2026, was fronted by a scarlet leopard with impeccable pitch and questionable taste in leather, and had spent just enough time in the modern production landscape to know where the sub-bass lives? NINE LIVES ON THE STRIP is not a hair-metal tribute act. It is a hair-metal record made by someone who genuinely loves the form and has the production chops to elevate it. The guitars are real (or close enough that the Marshall stacks don't know the difference). The vocals soar to the falsetto ceiling and growl in the chest-voice basement, sometimes within the same bar. The choruses are designed to be shouted back by ten thousand people — or one person in traffic. The fusion elements are surgical: three tracks incorporate EDM sub-bass and modern rhythmic texture, never more than 30% of any track's DNA. Two tracks are unmistakably modern in lyrical content — social media, AI, the cost of being authentic in 2026. The rest is pure 80s: power ballads, arena anthems, guitar solos that last exactly long enough to make you believe in something, and cat/kitty double-entendres that stay GFV-brand-safe while making the audience grin like they heard something they shouldn't have. St. Paul runs through the whole record: the seedy history, the warehouse artists, the Mississippi riverfront, the Wabasha Street clubs that have seen everything. Lowertown is not a backdrop — it is a character. The album's philosophical core, borrowed from the GFV playbook: you have nine lives, you are probably on your sixth, and every remaining one is worth turning up the volume for.

albums.title: MELANIE
albums.description: Single / developing album. The song Red Leopard never planned to write. After an entire debut of bravado, swagger, and controlled vulnerability, 'Melanie' is the thing he had no defense against: a woman in St. Paul who made him stop moving. An 80s power rock anthem that sounds like it was always part of the canon — Cathedral Hill at night, Cabernet on the counter, three cats, family calls, Montana roots, and a style that makes the city look like it dressed up for her. The key change on the final chorus (D to Eb) is the oldest trick in the playbook because it works. The nine-lives motif from the debut gets its deepest use: he'd trade them all for one more night beside her name.
